stem:
A 30-year-old attends a GP shared-care booking visit at nine weeks in her second pregnancy. Her blood donor card says she is group O, RhD positive. After her first birth she needed a two-unit red-cell transfusion for postpartum haemorrhage; that baby was well. She asks which blood test will show whether her immune system could attack this baby's red cells.

Which test answers her question?

options.label: A
options.text: No test, as an RhD-positive mother does not make harmful antibodies
options.explanation: RhD-positive women do not make anti-D, but they can form other antibodies such as anti-c, anti-E or anti-Kell, especially after a transfusion, and these can haemolyse fetal red cells.

options.label: B
options.text: A direct antiglobulin test performed on her own red cells
options.explanation: The direct antiglobulin test detects antibody already coating red cells. It is used on the baby's cells after birth, not to screen the mother's plasma.

options.label: C
options.text: A Kleihauer test to measure fetal cells in her circulation
options.explanation: A Kleihauer test sizes a fetomaternal bleed so anti-D can be dosed in an RhD-negative woman. It does not look for maternal antibodies.

options.label: D
options.text: Her blood group with a red-cell antibody screen of her plasma
options.explanation: Every woman has her blood group and an antibody screen at booking, whatever her RhD type. The screen detects circulating red-cell alloantibodies, and her past transfusion makes a non-D antibody more likely.

options.label: E
options.text: Cell-free fetal RHD genotyping on a maternal blood sample
options.explanation: Fetal RHD genotyping guides anti-D use in RhD-negative women. It says nothing about non-D antibodies in an RhD-positive mother.

context: Every pregnant woman, RhD positive or negative, has a blood group and red-cell antibody screen at booking; non-D antibodies, often after a transfusion, can cause fetal haemolysis.
